### Problem: Height Checker {#sec-lts-p1-a}

::: {.p-statement}

A line of students ($1 \le n \le 100$) stands at heights `heights[i]` ($1 \le \mathit{heights}[i] \le 100$). The photo wants them in non-decreasing order; let `expected` be that sorted arrangement. Return the number of indices where `heights[i] != expected[i]`.

Source: [LC 1051 · Height Checker](https://leetcode.com/problems/height-checker/){.solved difficulty="Easy"}

Example — `heights = [1, 1, 4, 2, 1, 3]`. Output `3` — sorted `expected = [1, 1, 1, 2, 3, 4]` differs at indices 2, 4, 5.
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
The obvious move is to sort and compare, $O(n \log n)$. But heights live in the tiny range $[1, 100]$: instead of *comparing* students we can just *tally* how many have each height and lay them back down from shortest to tallest. That is counting sort — $O(n + V)$ with $V = 100$ — and here the tally plus a single walk even lets us count the mismatches without materialising `expected`.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Sort and diff.** Copy the array, sort it, count positions where the two disagree. $O(n \log n)$ time, $O(n)$ space — the oracle.
2. **Counting sort.** Histogram the heights into `cnt[1..100]`, then read buckets low to high: the $j$-th emitted value is what `expected` would put at index $j$, so compare it to `heights[j]` on the fly. $O(n + V)$ time, $O(V)$ space.

**Invariant.** After filling `cnt`, `cnt[v]` is exactly how many students have height $v$; emitting in increasing $v$ therefore reproduces the sorted line position by position, so the running index $i$ always points at the next `expected` slot.
:::

The buttons are in order: pay for a comparison sort, then spend the small value range instead.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Sort and diff

::: {.form-next}
`expected` is just `sorted(heights)`; count the places they disagree. $O(n \log n)$ time, $O(n)$ extra space — correct and clear, and the baseline the histogram beats.

**Worked example.** $[1,1,4,2,1,3]$ vs $[1,1,1,2,3,4]$: equal at 0, 1, 3; differ at 2 ($4\ne1$), 4 ($1\ne3$), 5 ($3\ne4$) → $3$.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("hcheck", "brute")
    assert str(final) == "3"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def hc1051_sort(heights):
    exp = sorted(heights)
    return sum(1 for a, b in zip(heights, exp) if a != b)
```

##### C++

```cpp
// sort a copy, count mismatching positions, O(n log n)
int hc1051Sort(vector<int> heights) {
    vector<int> exp = heights;
    sort(exp.begin(), exp.end());
    int ans = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < (int)heights.size(); ++i)
        if (heights[i] != exp[i]) ++ans;
    return ans;
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** `sorted` is a comparison sort (Timsort in Python), so this tab is really @sec-salgo's tool used as the oracle. The `zip` pairs each original height with its sorted counterpart; the count of unequal pairs is the answer. It is $O(n \log n)$ for a problem whose numbers never leave $[1, 100]$ — which is exactly the situation counting sort was built to undercut.

#### Counting sort (histogram)

::: {.form-next}
Tally each height into `cnt[1..100]`, then walk $v = 1 \dots 100$ emitting `cnt[v]` copies of $v$. The running index $i$ is the position in the would-be sorted line, so compare `heights[i]` to $v$ as you emit — no `expected` array needed. $O(n + V)$ time, $O(V)$ space.

**Worked example.** `cnt[1]=3, cnt[2]=1, cnt[3]=1, cnt[4]=1`. Emit $1,1,1,2,3,4$ and compare to $1,1,4,2,1,3$: mismatches at the three slots as before → $3$.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("hcheck", "count")
    assert str(final) == "3"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: arr-lts-1051-count
def hc1051_count(heights):
    cnt = [0] * 101
    for v in heights:
        cnt[v] += 1
    ans = 0
    i = 0
    for v in range(1, 101):
        for _ in range(cnt[v]):
            if heights[i] != v:
                ans += 1
            i += 1
    return ans

for _ in range(400):
    h = [random.randint(1, 100) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 25))]
    assert hc1051_count(h) == hc1051_sort(h)
assert hc1051_count([1, 1, 4, 2, 1, 3]) == 3
assert hc1051_count([5, 1, 2, 3, 4]) == 5
assert hc1051_count([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]) == 0
print("hc1051_count OK")
```

##### C++

```cpp
// counting sort by height value, O(n + V) time, O(V) space
int hc1051Count(vector<int> heights) {
    vector<int> cnt(101, 0);
    for (int v : heights) ++cnt[v];
    int ans = 0, i = 0;
    for (int v = 1; v <= 100; ++v)
        for (int k = 0; k < cnt[v]; ++k)
            if (heights[i++] != v) ++ans;
    return ans;
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** The histogram turn makes *value* into *address*: `cnt[v]` is the bucket for height $v$, and the inner `for _ in range(cnt[v])` emits exactly that many copies, so `i` marches through the sorted order without us ever building it. When the value range ($100$) is no bigger than $n \log n$, the counting pass wins. Stability does not matter here: the emitted values are bare numbers, and two equal heights are indistinguishable, so this histogram form of @sec-lts-a1 is enough; records with payloads would need the stable placement of @sec-lts-a2.

:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Sort + diff** is $O(n \log n)$ time, $O(n)$ space. **Counting sort** is $O(n + V)$ time, $O(V)$ space with $V = 100$ — $O(n + 100)$ here, so effectively linear. The histogram is the cheaper purchase whenever the value range stays small.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- Already sorted (`[1,2,3,4,5]`) → $0$ mismatches; every emitted bucket aligns with the input.
- All equal (`[3,3,3]`) → $0$; one bucket holds everything.
- $n = 1$ → always $0$; a single student is trivially "sorted".
:::

::: {.practice}
- [CF 651B · Beautiful Paintings](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/651/B){rating="1200"} — values at most $1000$: one histogram, and the answer is $n$ minus the largest count.
- [LC 2037 · Minimum Number of Moves to Seat Everyone](https://leetcode.com/problems/minimum-number-of-moves-to-seat-everyone/){difficulty="Easy"} — values at most $100$: counting-sort both lists and pair them in order.
:::
